coverageActuallyRead.source: Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History II.29–30, New Advent
coverageActuallyRead.locator: HTML chapter headings and paragraphs, lines 318–331 (New Advent page 26022, Book II, not page 26023)
coverageActuallyRead.read: Read Sozomen's account of Arius returning from Egypt to Constantinople, the planned communion/readmission, Alexander's opposition, Arius' death in a public place, and competing contemporary interpretations. Chapter 30 attributes an alternate narrative to Athanasius.

Read the passage in which Athanasius says Eusebius pressed him to readmit Arius, Constantine sent an order, and Athanasius refused. This passage establishes pressure concerning communion; it does not narrate Arius' death or independently verify the alleged toilet death.

coverageActuallyRead.source: Ellen Muehlberger, 'The Legend of Arius’ Death: Imagination, Space and Filth in Late Ancient Historiography', Past & Present 227.1
coverageActuallyRead.locator: Open-access article lines 65, 77–95, 126; no print-page/PDF page number was displayed in the consulted web view
coverageActuallyRead.read: Read discussion that fifth-century church histories follow a story attributed earlier to Athanasius but vary its meaning/details; author explicitly advises treating the story as rumor rather than secure historical report and analyzes its later Theodosian-era public-space/polemical development.

coverageActuallyRead.source: Timothy Barnes, 'The Exile and Recalls of Arius', Journal of Theological Studies 60.1 (2009)
coverageActuallyRead.read: Only the abstract was accessible/read. Barnes argues for a recall in 335 and death in 336; full argument/article was not accessed, so this is not represented as a full-text reading.

episodes.supportedClaims: Sozomen's fifth-century account reports a Constantinople setting and an anticipated readmission/communion shortly before Arius died. Athanasius' text independently supports prior conflict over whether Arius should be admitted to communion. Modern accessible scholarship identifies the bodily-death story as a rumor-shaped, polemical tradition; Barnes' abstract supports 336 as a defended chronology.
episodes.unsupportedOrDisputed: The cause and graphic circumstances of death, divine punishment, magical killing, and a planned procession/readmission as secure fact are not verified by contemporary neutral evidence. Sozomen himself reports that people interpreted the death differently and gives conflicting explanations. The exact day/date is not supplied in Sozomen II.29–30. The candidate URL 26023 is the wrong book (Book III); correct Sozomen Book II page is 26022. Sozomen II.29–30 contains the relevant account; II.29 heading is on page 26022.
episodes.chronologyAndPlace: Sozomen narrates events following the Synod of Jerusalem and Arius' return from Egypt; the passage alone does not date that sequence to a numbered year. Secondary chronology commonly assigns death to 336; Barnes' abstract argues 336, and Muehlberger cites that dating. Constantinople is named by the text, but the public latrine's exact historical site is not securely established by this consultation. Socrates' more elaborate Forum/colonnade location is a distinct later version and should not be merged into Sozomen's wording.
episodes.biasAndLimits: Athanasius was a direct participant in the doctrinal conflict and an interested polemical author. Sozomen wrote in the fifth century and frames the story providentially, although he preserves disagreement. Muehlberger's article argues directly that the death narrative should be analyzed as rumor and later historiographic construction. No archaeological place or exact forum/latrine footprint was established.

coverageActuallyRead.source: Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.61–66, New Advent
coverageActuallyRead.locator: HTML ch. 61–66, lines 246–271; NPNF2 vol. 1 English translation; no scanned page image or printed pagination was consulted
coverageActuallyRead.read: IV.61–62: illness, baths, Helenopolis, suburbs of Nicomedia, bishops summoned and baptism, but the officiating bishop is not named. IV.63: inheritance apportioned among children. IV.64: death at midday on the final day of Pentecost, without a numbered calendar date. IV.66: body carried from Nicomedia to Constantinople.

coverageActuallyRead.locator: Online translated Chronicle, year 337 lines 1976–1984 in the HTML transcription
coverageActuallyRead.read: The annal explicitly says Constantine was baptized at the end of life by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and gives a theological/polemical conclusion that he fell into Arian doctrine. The text also has a separate chronicle notice placing his death at a public villa near Nicomedia, but its year-column placement and chronology do not constitute an eyewitness diary.

coverageActuallyRead.source: Jan Drijvers book review, Bryn Mawr Classical Review (2006)
coverageActuallyRead.read: Read review's summary of Eusebius and later western baptism traditions. It notes that Eusebius names no baptizer; Jerome is the earliest source to identify Eusebius of Nicomedia (late fourth century), and the Nicomedian suburb/villa Achyron identification is probable rather than certain. This is a review, not the monograph itself.

episodes.supportedClaims: Eusebius' near-contemporary biography reports Constantine's final illness, baptism in the suburbs of Nicomedia, death on Pentecost, and transport of the body to Constantinople. Jerome's later fourth-century chronicle explicitly identifies the baptizer as Eusebius of Nicomedia and associates the baptism with 337.
episodes.unsupportedOrDisputed: The exact date 22 May is not in Eusebius IV.61–64; Eusebius gives Pentecost but no Julian calendar date. The chronicle year and Pentecost calculation support conventional dating, while later chronologies sometimes differ by a day. Eusebius does not name the officiating bishop; do not cite VC IV.61–64 alone as proving Eusebius of Nicomedia performed baptism. The specific estate/villa name Achyron is an identification from other testimony/scholarship, not named in Eusebius' passage. The later Sylvester baptism story is not evidence for this event and is a separate tradition.
episodes.chronologyAndPlace: Eusebius says Constantine travelled from his own city/Constantinople to Helenopolis, then proceeded to Nicomedia's suburbs. He does not specify an exact bath, church, palace, or estate. Death is on Pentecost's concluding day in his account. The 22 May date is conventional and supported by later calendrical calculation; Jerome's year 337 is explicit.
episodes.geographyAndBuildings: Nicomedia is modern İzmit in broad gazetteer identifications; the search result for Pleiades place 511337 did not expose its page due bot protection, so its coordinates were not directly checked in the record. No archaeological/institutional excavation report fixing the suburbs, hot-bath site, or villa was read. Present-day İzmit coordinates should not be used as a precise 337 residence footprint. Helenopolis is named in the narrative, but its precise stop/bath location was not validated here. No claims about buildings constructed in 337 are supported by the passage.
episodes.biasAndLimits: Eusebius' Vita is an imperial Christian encomium that presents the emperor's final actions devotionally and supplies reconstructed speeches; do not present its speech as stenographic. Jerome is later and explicitly turns baptizer identity into an Arian polemic. Eusebius omits the baptizer's name. The online New Advent/NPNF translation is a 19th-century English text; web locators are chapter/paragraphs, not printed page numbers. PDF page index was not used, so no PDF/printed-page equivalence is asserted.

coverageActuallyRead.source: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History II.2 and II.25, New Advent
coverageActuallyRead.locator: Book II, ch. 2 lines 16–24; ch. 25 lines 272–277 (HTML; printed pagination not consulted)
coverageActuallyRead.read: II.2 reports that after Constantine's death Constantius held the eastern share assigned by his father's will; describes court/doctrinal factional changes. II.25 says Dalmatius shared imperial authority briefly and soldiers killed him, while Constantius neither ordered nor forbade the killing; it also summarizes Constantine II's later incursion/death.

Read Latin and notes: Constantine left three sons and one brother's son; Dalmatius was soon overthrown by a military faction with Constantius allowing rather than ordering it; Constantine II's later death in conflict near Aquileia is separate.

coverageActuallyRead.source: R. W. Burgess, 'The Summer of Blood: The Great Massacre of 337 and the Promotion of the Sons of Constantine', Dumbarton Oaks Papers 62 (2008)
coverageActuallyRead.locator: Selected printed journal14–15; physicalPDF11–12, zero-based10–11; actual architect-download running page labels checked
coverageActuallyRead.read: Architect read source-dependence discussion and note45, official explanations and alternative accusations. Initial delegated page-pair assertion was incorrect: zero-index10 is printed14, not15. Original source dependence is a modern argument, not independent multiple contemporary witnesses.

episodes.supportedClaims: Sources report that Constantine left sons and a nephew in succession arrangements; Socrates says Dalmatius briefly shared imperial authority, then soldiers killed him, with Constantius neither ordering nor preventing it. Eutropius and the Epitome likewise attribute Dalmatius' killing to a military faction/violence. Constantine II's death in 340 near Aquileia is a later separate conflict, not part of the 337 death episode.
episodes.unsupportedOrDisputed: Socrates and Eutropius do not establish a complete massacre list of all male relatives, the exact chain of command, or an uncontested motive. Later accounts accuse Constantius more directly; Eutropius' wording says he permitted rather than ordered it. Burgess argues that several surviving reports derive from a single lost source tradition, so apparent multiple attestations are not fully independent. The sources do not support a permanent constitutional partition finalized at the instant of Constantine's death. They describe allocations/authority and later political developments; precise formal settlement dates require additional evidence. Do not narrate private motives or invented dispatches as fact.
episodes.chronologyAndPlace: Event occurs in 337 after Constantine's death. Eusebius IV.63 gives a general division of inheritance but not named regional allocations. Socrates II.2 attributes the East to Constantius in the will; the Epitome's detailed shares include Dalmatius and Hannibalianus. The murder's exact day and site are not specified in the consulted passages; Constantinople is the court context, not a proven assassination location. Constantine II's later death is associated by Socrates with incursion into Constans' region; Eutropius identifies conflict at Aquileia, around 340.
episodes.biasAndLimits: Socrates is a fifth-century Christian historian and openly describes doctrinal conflict from a Nicene perspective. Eutropius is a fourth-century imperial breviary; its compressed account has political phrasing. Epitome de Caesaribus is anonymous/uncertain authorship and later than Aurelius Victor despite common misattribution. Burgess' source analysis cautions against counting derivative accounts as independent corroboration.
